rationale:
Today's quota is 1 long, 3 Shorts and 0 carousels. Every piece is about GLP-1 and follows the 10-27 growth playbook.

**Long-form (L1).** This is the first Lane A video in the playbook's order: tirzepatide, bones and muscle. It's the default slot and our best earner (practical tirzepatide videos average about 125 minutes, about 2.4× the channel median). The evidence is settled and has been checked before: SURMOUNT-1's body-scan substudy, the Archives of Osteoporosis systematic review and well-documented weight-loss biology. That suits a long video that has to pass the fact-check. Our bones (235 views) and muscle (133) Shorts show demand. It's a new angle for a long-form; the 10-16 strength video was a "where to start" training guide.

**Why the tradipitant news isn't the long-form.** It's the one result inside the 48-hour window, but it doesn't meet the Lane C bar. It's an add-on anti-sickness pill, not a next-gen GLP-1. It used a single-dose challenge model, and so far there's only a press release and trade-press coverage. The fact-check would likely fail a long script built on that. It goes to the 13:00 Short instead (momentum 88, low competition).

**Shorts.**
- **08:00 (S1):** a calm "honest uncertainty" Short on tirzepatide hair loss, built on the new systematic review. Our GLP-1 hair long-form was 9-28, outside the 30-day window.
- **13:00 (S2):** the tradipitant result, framed carefully because the radar marked it `caution`.
- **20:00 (S3):** the Exp D funnel Short and the spin-off of L1. It asks a new question ("does losing more weight mean losing more muscle?") from the 10-15 J Clin Med cohort.

**What I skipped and why.**
- ACOG pregnancy: we ran a Short on 10-24.
- TRIUMPH-OSA: already used in a Short on 10-24 (limit of one Short per trial per week).
- Lilly earnings: they're tomorrow, so this is a watch item for a possible Lane C video on 10-29/30.
- Gray-market recall: the topic has low reach on Instagram, and today's slots went to stronger topics.
- Plateau and stopping: both were long-forms on 10-27.

**Balance.** Body systems: muscle and bone (2), digestion and nausea (1), hair and skin (1), so no three on one system. Pillars: get-the-most ×2, myths, research. Mix: emerging news (S2), evergreen with a fresh hook (L1, S3), and a calm myth correction (S1).

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and your bones and muscle: how much of the weight lost is lean mass, what the evidence does and doesn't show about bone, and the guideline habits that help protect both
pieces.angle:
Lane A (log 'lane: A'), 'Life on Tirzepatide' series, 8–12 min, 14:00 ET. The first spoken sentence answers the title in plain words, using a 'you' scenario: 'You're losing weight on tirzepatide, so is some of it muscle and bone? Some of it is lean mass, as with any weight loss. The bone evidence is still thin, and the habits that help are well established.'

Chapters named after searched questions:
(1) Does tirzepatide cause muscle loss? Use the SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy: about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass. Give per-arm sizes and 72 weeks from the paper. Population: adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Lean mass isn't pure muscle.
(2) Does losing more weight mean losing more muscle? J Clin Med, Oct 15, 2026: observational, muscle estimated by a device. Name the exact drugs and population the paper covered.
(3) Does tirzepatide affect bone density? Archives of Osteoporosis systematic review, Oct 23, 2026: 8 small RCTs, mostly exenatide and liraglutide, 1 semaglutide trial, no tirzepatide, very low certainty, fracture trials needed. Confirm all of this against the abstract. Add tirzepatide bone data only from a verified primary paper.
(4) Why weight loss by any method can affect bone and muscle: established biology from diet and bariatric studies, labelled as separate studies.
(5) What helps? Guideline habits, marked 'recommended', not 'proven on tirzepatide': muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week, started gently; a protein food at each meal unless your clinician limits protein (for example, kidney disease).
(6) Who should ask about bone health? People with osteoporosis, fracture risk, or who are older or post-menopausal: questions for your clinician.

Re-hook every 45–75 s. One GI line. One subscribe ask, after the 'what helps' payoff. Say 'don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. No dosing.

Ending: speak no titles. Say 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher links Strength Training on Tirzepatide.

Thumbnail: 4 words or fewer, e.g. 'Keep Your Strength', with a calm labelled character. No scary skeleton.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and hair loss: how common shedding is and why it's usually temporary (Med Sci (Basel) systematic review of skin side effects, Oct 9, 2026)
pieces.angle:
08:00 calm 'honest uncertainty' body-worry Short, 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer.

Open within 10 s: 'Hairbrush looking fuller on tirzepatide? Hair shedding has been reported, and it's often temporary shedding linked to fast weight loss (telogen effluvium).'

Use the review's verified findings only, scoped to the drugs it covered (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide). Give any trial rates per arm against placebo, exactly as published. Observational relative risks get 'linked to' and their absolute context.

What helps: enough protein (with the kidney caveat), and ask your doctor about checking iron, thyroid and vitamin D. See a dermatologist if shedding lasts more than about 6 months, comes in patches, or is painful. No supplement promises.

One GI line. 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. End with 'follow for more'. No emoji, captions mix at 0.02 or lower.

pieces.topic: A pill to prevent GLP-1 vomiting? Tradipitant Phase 3 Study 3601 after a single semaglutide dose (Vanda, Oct 27, 2026)
pieces.angle: Hook: 'Can a pill stop GLP-1 vomiting before it starts? A new Phase 3 trial tested one.' Credit: 'Vanda, Oct 27, 2026; company-reported, not peer-reviewed.' Numbers: any vomiting 43.0% (61 of 142) on tradipitant vs 58.5% (96 of 164) on placebo, after one semaglutide dose given without the usual gradual start, so it's a stress test and not how real treatment begins. Status: tradipitant is approved in the US for motion-sickness vomiting, but not for GLP-1 vomiting; Vanda plans to file. No tirzepatide data. Mechanism: it blocks NK-1 signals in the brain's vomiting centre. What helps today: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full, sipping fluids; tell your prescriber about vomiting that keeps going; don't take any anti-sickness medicine for this without your prescriber. 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line, with a loop ending. Title: 'Semaglutide Vomiting: Could a Pill Prevent It?'
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide Nausea: Could a Pill Prevent the Vomiting?
pieces.why: The freshest randomized result on the radar (Oct 27, momentum 88, low competition). It speaks to the top worry of GLP-1 users, but it's too new and press-release-only for a long video. | fact-check: The trial exists and the numbers check out. Vanda press release, 27 Oct 2026: Study 3601, Phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled; any vomiting 43.0% (61/142) vs 58.5% (96/164), p=0.006; all participants got a single 1 mg semaglutide dose without titration; an sNDA is planned; 'generally well tolerated'. Problems: (1) NCT06804603 is the earlier Phase 2 trial (124 enrolled, BMI 25–40, diabetes excluded), not Study 3601. Don't take Study 3601's population from it. The press release doesn't state the population, so say only 'adults given a single semaglutide dose'. (2) Tradipitant (NEREUS) has been FDA-approved since 30 Dec 2025 for preventing motion-sickness vomiting. 'Not approved' is therefore inaccurate. The correct line is 'approved in the US for motion sickness, not for GLP-1 vomiting'. Add 'don't take it or any anti-sickness medicine for this without your prescriber', so the Short doesn't encourage off-label self-use. (3) The hook 'Just started a GLP-1 and the nausea hit?' implies it treats existing nausea in real patients. The trial tested prevention after one untitrated dose, so reframe the hook. (4) Give the relative reduction only next to the absolute numbers. Company-reported, not peer-reviewed. No tirzepatide data. Sources: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/vanda-pharmaceuticals-announces-positive-results-from-study-3601-of-nereus-tradipitant-for-prevention-of-glp-1induced-vomiting-302920054.html ; https://www.hcplive.com/view/tradipitant-cuts-semaglutide-induced-vomiting-in-phase-3-trial ; https://www.hcplive.com/view/fda-approves-tradipitant-nereus-for-the-prevention-of-vomiting-induced-by-motion

pieces.topic: Does losing more weight on tirzepatide mean losing more muscle? Weight-loss size, fat mass and device-estimated muscle loss (J Clin Med, Oct 15, 2026)
pieces.angle: Title if the paper has a tirzepatide-specific result: 'Tirzepatide: Does Losing More Weight Mean Losing More Muscle?' Otherwise: 'GLP-1 Weight Loss: Does Losing More Mean Losing More Muscle?' Then say 'in people on obesity medicines, including tirzepatide'. Open with the paper's verified finding, labelled 'observational, muscle estimated by a device, not a trial', and name the exact drugs and population the paper covered. Add one SURMOUNT-1 anchor ('in a body-scan substudy, about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass, which isn't all muscle') that matches L1 word for word. Then two recommended habits: strength training started gently, and protein at each meal unless your clinician limits it. One GI line. 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Does Losing More Weight Mean Losing More Muscle?
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 and the 20:00 Exp D funnel Short pointing to today's bones and muscle long-form. Our muscle Shorts are proven performers. | fact-check: Confirmed that the paper exists: J Clin Med 2026;15(20):8008, 'Weight-Loss Magnitude, Fat Mass, and Device-Estimated Muscle Mass Loss During Obesity Pharmacotherapy', https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/20/8008. The full text returned 403, so I couldn't confirm which drugs, which population or which tirzepatide-specific result it covers. The paper's title says 'obesity pharmacotherapy', not tirzepatide. The working title puts tirzepatide on a finding that may come from a mixed-drug cohort, which breaks the scope rule. Keep tirzepatide in the title only if the content checker confirms the paper reports a tirzepatide-specific result. Otherwise use the generic title below. Muscle was device-estimated, so it is observational, 'linked to', not causal. The SURMOUNT-1 anchor must match L1's verified figures exactly. Funnel target: L1 publishes at 14:00, before the 20:00 slot, but the publisher must confirm L1 is live before linking. Keep the protein kidney caveat.
